items.stem:
QUALITY RELEASE RECORD
A manufacturer's label declares that a drug contains ingredient A. Laboratory confirmation establishes that ingredient B was substituted for A in the finished batch. No issue with package cleanliness is alleged. Which federal adulteration provision independently addresses this substitution?

choices.text: 21 U.S.C. §351(d)(2): substitution of another substance.
choices.why: Correct. Substituting another substance wholly or in part is an independent adulteration ground under FD&C Act section 501(d)(2).

choices.text: 21 U.S.C. §352(c), failure to make required label text conspicuous.
choices.why: Incorrect. The presented defect is the substituted substance, not how prominently required labeling appears.

choices.text: 21 U.S.C. §352(b), omission of the manufacturer's place of business.
choices.why: Incorrect. The scenario does not identify a missing manufacturer address.

choices.text: 21 U.S.C. §351(a)(3), a poisonous drug container.
choices.why: Incorrect. No poisonous container is described, although the product itself has an adulteration defect.

items.citation: 21 U.S.C. §351(d)(2); 21 U.S.C. §352(a)(1) may additionally apply if labeling is false
items.novelty_rationale: Ingredient substitution rather than E30-108's insanitary conditions, compendial assay, or material label claim.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem: A pharmacy receives an unopened drug lot whose tablets pass potency and purity assays. The inner packaging contains a confirmed toxic coating capable of leaching into the tablets and rendering them injurious. Which statements follow the federal adulteration provisions? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The passing tablet assay proves that the package is safe for patient use.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 U.S.C. §351(a)(3) addresses potentially injurious containers independent of an assay of contents.

choices.text: A harmful container can establish adulteration even if tablets initially pass assay.
choices.why: Correct. A poisonous or deleterious drug container capable of rendering contents injurious meets section 501(a)(3).

choices.text: A recall announcement must occur before a hazardous container can be treated as adulterated.
choices.why: Incorrect. Statutory adulteration does not require a previously announced recall.

choices.text: The pharmacy should not assume initial tablet assays negate the container risk.
choices.why: Correct. Container-related adulteration is a separate fact from tested tablet strength or purity.

items.novelty_rationale: Poisonous drug-container provision untested by E30-108's held-insanitary/storage and label/potency facts.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem: An FDA-required prescription warning appears on the manufacturer's carton in tiny, low-contrast lettering, although the text is technically present. Which distinct FD&C Act misbranding provision directly addresses whether it can readily be read and understood?

choices.text: Section 502(i): an imitation drug name.
choices.why: Incorrect. There is no competing branded imitation in the facts.

choices.text: Section 501(d): ingredient substitution.
choices.why: Incorrect. No ingredient substitution is described.

choices.text: Section 502(c): required label text lacks prominence.
choices.why: Correct. Section 502(c), 21 U.S.C. §352(c), addresses conspicuous placement and ordinary readability.

choices.text: Section 501(a)(3), because the drug container has poisonous material.
choices.why: Incorrect. Typography is not evidence of a poisonous container.

items.novelty_rationale: Tests conspicuous required labeling rather than E30-323's materially false therapeutic claim.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem:
CONTAINER INSPECTION
A manufacturer fills a very large opaque bottle with a small quantity of tablets and constructs a deceptive viewing chamber that makes the contents appear far more numerous. The printed numerical count is accurate. Which federal issue remains relevant?

choices.text: An automatic violation of federal controlled-substance inventory requirements.
choices.why: Incorrect. Misleading retail presentation is not, by itself, a controlled inventory discrepancy.

choices.text: No misbranding issue because the numerical count is correct.
choices.why: Incorrect. A truthful count does not eliminate the distinct prohibition on a misleading container.

choices.text: A failed potency assay is needed for a product defect.
choices.why: Incorrect. Misleading packaging can be misbranding without an assay failure.

choices.text: Section 502(i)(1), a drug container made or filled so as to be misleading.
choices.why: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §352(i)(1) independently treats a misleading container as misbranding.

items.novelty_rationale: New packaging deception ground despite truthful quantity declaration; not E30-108/C083 false-label recognition.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem:
DSCSA SUSPECT-PRODUCT INVESTIGATION
A dispenser holds 60 identical suspect prescription-drug packages from one implicated shipment. Under the federal minimum product-identifier sampling rule, how many packages must be verified in the investigation, assuming no applicable relief?

choices.text: Three packages, because the three-unit threshold controls.
choices.why: Incorrect. When ten percent of the suspect packages exceeds three, the higher count applies.

choices.text: Six packages, because ten percent exceeds the three-package minimum.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(4)(A)(ii)(II) requires at least three packages or 10%, whichever is greater.

choices.text: One package for each manufacturer in the shipment.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statutory sample requirement is not simply one item per manufacturer.

choices.text: All sixty packages even when a qualifying minimum sample can be used.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cited investigation sampling provision specifies a threshold of at least three or ten percent, whichever is greater.

items.novelty_rationale: Quantitative package-level verification not tested by E30-030 general quarantine/notification questions.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem: A dispenser completes the disposition of a product confirmed to be illegitimate, following the applicable investigation and notification steps. For how long must it keep the federal records of that DISPOSITION, measured from the conclusion of disposition?

choices.text: At least six years from the conclusion of disposition.
choices.why: Correct. 21 U.S.C. §360eee-1(d)(4)(B)(v) uses the end of disposition as the retention clock for those records.

choices.text: Two business days after the initial manufacturer alert.
choices.why: Incorrect. Two business days concerns certain official requests for tracing records, not the disposition-retention period.

choices.text: Until the next routine controlled-substance inventory.
choices.why: Incorrect. The disposition record requirement does not end on the pharmacy inventory date.

choices.text: Six months from the original purchase order.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither the duration nor the starting point matches the specific federal rule.

items.novelty_rationale: Tests a DIFFERENT six-year clock (illegitimate disposition), not E30-030's suspect investigation records.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem: An appropriate state or federal official requests the transaction information, statement, and history received by a pharmacy to investigate an illegitimate prescription drug. Assume no applicable relief or special alternative deadline was set. What is required? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacy may defer a response until its ordinary annual inventory.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statutory clock for a qualifying official request is much shorter.

choices.text: The pharmacy must respond no later than two business days after the qualifying request.
choices.why: Correct. Section 582(d)(1)(D) sets a two-business-day deadline unless an alternate reasonable time is determined based on the request.

choices.text: A written third-party storage arrangement removes the dispenser's legal duty to respond.
choices.why: Incorrect. A recordkeeping service does not release the dispenser from its statutory obligations.

choices.text: The pharmacy must supply the applicable received tracing records, subject to statutory scope.
choices.why: Correct. An appropriate official can request the transaction information, statement and history received from the prior owner.

items.novelty_rationale: Records-production deadline to an investigating government official, not E30-163's general vendor retention obligation.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem: An authorized physician treats patients in an office and directly administers covered prescription medication during ordinary professional practice. No pharmacy or outside wholesaler transfers ownership as part of the physician's own act of administration. Which DSCSA dispenser provision addresses this practitioner?

choices.text: All community pharmacy tracing requirements apply to the physician simply because a drug is administered.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 582(d)(5) expressly treats covered practitioners separately in the ordinary course of professional practice.

choices.text: The exception waives FDA drug quality laws for physicians.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statute exempts certain DSCSA subsections, not adulteration, misbranding, or quality requirements.

choices.text: Section 582(d)(5) excepts qualifying practitioners from specified dispenser tracing and verification duties.
choices.why: Correct. The statute excepts eligible licensed practitioners and supervised licensed individuals from subsections (d)(1) and (d)(4).

choices.text: The office must become a licensed wholesale distributor before giving one clinic-administered dose.
choices.why: Incorrect. Routine lawful practitioner administration is not automatically wholesale distribution.

items.novelty_rationale: Practitioner-specific statutory exemption, not E30-075 small dispenser business qualification or C120 patient-specific transfer.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem:
FDA STATUS SNAPSHOT — November 2026
Product: Paxlovid. FDA has approved treatment for qualifying high-risk adults. Its COVID-19 EUA separately covers qualifying pediatric patients aged at least 12 years and weighing at least 40 kg. Which regulatory statement follows?

choices.text: Adult approval extends to pediatric use.
choices.why: Incorrect. The authorized pediatric use is under the separate EUA, not the adult approved indication.

choices.text: The pediatric EUA means the medicine has no FDA-approved indication in any age group.
choices.why: Incorrect. FDA has approved a specified adult COVID-19 use.

choices.text: The EUA independently permits any pediatric age and body weight if the prescriber documents severity.
choices.why: Incorrect. The authorized pediatric population has specified age, weight and risk criteria.

choices.text: Use the adult approval or the pediatric EUA terms, as applicable.
choices.why: Correct. FDA approval for qualifying adults and EUA for specified pediatric patients coexist.

items.citation: 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3(a)(2)-(3); FDA current Paxlovid approval/EUA entries (November 2026)
items.novelty_rationale: Actual approved adult versus pediatric EUA split not tested by C's REMS comparisons.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.

items.stem: An inpatient team proposes Gohibic (vilobelimab) under its COVID-19 EUA for a hospitalized adult whose invasive mechanical ventilation began 62 hours earlier. The FDA authorization describes initiation within 48 hours after ventilation or ECMO begins. No other lawful access route is established. What should the pharmacist conclude?

choices.text: It is FDA-approved for ventilated adults.
choices.why: Incorrect. The cited FDA COVID-19 pathway is an EUA, not general approval without a time condition.

choices.text: A high-risk adult status alone substitutes for the EUA's ventilation-time condition.
choices.why: Incorrect. The EUA imposes a timing window beyond patient age and hospitalization.

choices.text: Initiation at 62 hours is outside this EUA's 48-hour window.
choices.why: Correct. FDA lists Gohibic EUA use for hospitalized adults when initiated within 48 hours of starting IMV or ECMO.

choices.text: The FDA EUA starts the 48-hour clock at the pharmacy's first purchase of Gohibic.
choices.why: Incorrect. The clock refers to the patient's start of invasive mechanical ventilation or ECMO.

items.citation: 21 U.S.C. §360bbb-3; FDA Gohibic authorized use, April 2026 amendment
items.novelty_rationale: Uses an actual named drug's EUA timing condition rather than generic 'clinical need' exception.
items.copyright_policy: Original educational scenario; not actual secure MPJE question.
